hints: Focus on what 'X2 formed' really means, a halogen molecule can only appear if its halide ion has given away electrons.
Notice that Y2 oxidises both X- and Z- to their halogens, while X2 oxidises nothing at all.
Remember the strongest oxidising halogen makes the weakest reducing halide ion, so flip the halogen order to get the halide order.
walkthrough:
**Understand what a reaction tells us**

Think of halogen displacement as a competition for electrons. If we see a new halogen formed, the added halogen has stolen electrons.

$$\text{halogen} + \text{halide ion} \rightarrow \text{new halogen} + \text{new halide ion}$$

**Rank the halogens as oxidising agents**

Look down each row. $X_2$ does nothing, so it is the weakest oxidiser. $Z_2$ oxidises only $X^-$ to $X_2$, so it is in the middle. $Y_2$ oxidises both $X^-$ to $X_2$ and $Z^-$ to $Z_2$, so it is the strongest.

$$\text{oxidising strength: } Y_2 > Z_2 > X_2$$

**Flip the order for reducing agents**

A strong oxidiser gains electrons easily, so its own ion loses electrons with difficulty. That means the order of reducing strength of the ions is the reverse.

$$\text{reducing strength: } X^- > Z^- > Y^-$$

**Pick the strongest to weakest order**

$X^-$ is oxidised by both $Y_2$ and $Z_2$, so it gives up electrons most easily and is strongest. $Y^-$ is never oxidised, so it is weakest. This gives strongest $X^-$, then $Z^-$, then weakest $Y^-$.

options.A: This puts Y- in the middle, but Y- is never oxidised by X2, Y2 or Z2. That shows Y- holds its electrons most tightly, so it must be the weakest reducing agent, not the middle one.
options.B: Correct and well done. X- is oxidised twice (by Y2 and Z2) so it is the strongest reducer. Z- is oxidised once (by Y2) so it is in the middle. Y- is never oxidised so it is the weakest. Order X- > Z- > Y- matches oxidising order Y2 > Z2 > X2 reversed.
options.C: This reverses the chemistry. Y2 displaces both X2 and Z2, proving Y2 is the strongest oxidiser, so Y- must be the weakest reducer, not the strongest. Students who choose this have confused oxidising strength with reducing strength.
options.D: This correctly puts Y- weakest but swaps X- and Z-. Z2 oxidises X- to X2 ($Z_2 + 2X^- \rightarrow X_2 + 2Z^-$), proving X- loses electrons more easily than Z-, so X- is stronger than Z-, not weaker.
